newsitem.title: UK: Agencies condemn cut in Britain's overseas aid.
newsitem.headline: Agencies condemn cut in Britain's overseas aid.

text.p: Aid agencies condemned deep cuts in Britain's overseas aid announced in Tuesday's budget, saying the world's poor were being forced to help pay for tax cuts announced by finance minister Kenneth Clarke.

The budget for the Overseas Development Administration (ODA) will drop 8.4 percent in 1997/98, after adjusting for inflation, to 1.96 billion pounds ($3.3 billion) -- the second reduction in as many years.
"Today's tax cuts have been squeezed out of the lives of the poor," Barry Coates, director of the World Development Movement, said in a statement.

He estimated that Britain's aid as a percentage of gross domestic product would drop to a new low next year of 0.24 percent -- well below the United Nations target of 0.7 percent and down from a high of 0.51 percent in 1979, the year the ruling Conservative Party won power.

Julian Filochowski, director of the Roman Catholic charity CAFOD, expressed dismay at the cut on behalf of a coalition of British aid agencies. He called on the government and parliament to think again.
"Following last year's cut this represents a continued war of attrition against the world's poor," Filochowski said in a statement. "Is this the hallmark of a civilised nation?"
The ODA put on a brave face, saying the government had reaffirmed its commitment to a substantial development programme aimed at improving the quality of life of the world's poor.

One winner in the budget was the World Service of the British Broadcasting Corporation, which won an extra five million pounds following intensive lobbying by members of parliament and leading opinion makers.

World Service managing director Sam Younger said the additional money would not only stave off the threat of further reductions in foreign-language services but would enable it to invest in new areas.

The network of the British Council, which promotes the English language and British culture overseas, will also be protected from closures as a result of a four million pound increase in its budget next year, the Foreign Office said. ($1=.5990 Pound)
